screens.title: Service Discovery and API Gateways
screens.narratorSegment: In modern microservice systems, service endpoints are fluid: instances come and go, and network addresses change continually. Service discovery is the mechanism that solves the core question: how does one service learn the current location of another? In parallel, an A P I Gateway provides a single, stable entry point for external clients, handling routing, security, aggregation, and operational controls so client code stays simple. This lesson will help you understand both concerns and why they belong in every production microservice design. We'll ground the ideas with concrete examples: how a service registers itself when it starts, how a client selects a healthy instance, and how a mobile app can ask one gateway for a dashboard composed from several services. I'll also point out common pitfalls, such as hardcoding addresses, overloading the gateway with business logic, or creating a single point of failure. By the end, you should see how service registries, discovery clients, and A P I Gateways work together to enable resilient, evolvable systems, and be ready to choose patterns that match your operational constraints.

screens.title: What is Service Discovery?
screens.narratorSegment: Service discovery is the runtime process by which services locate each other in a distributed system. The definition is simple: instead of hardcoding IP addresses and ports, services publish where they run to a registry, and other services query that registry to learn how to reach them. This matters because microservice instances are ephemeral. They scale up and down, crash and restart, and move across hosts or containers. Without discovery, every change would require manual configuration updates, which is error-prone and slow. A concrete example is a User Service registering its address and port with a registry when it starts. An Order Service querying the registry gets a current list of healthy User Service instances and chooses one to call. A common misconception is that service discovery only stores addresses; in practice, registries also manage health checks and metadata so clients can choose healthy instances. Takeaway: discovery decouples service identity from location, enabling independent scaling and resilient connections. Consider: what operational signals will you require in health checks to avoid false positives when an instance is overloaded but not failed?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Service discovery dynamically maps logical service names to live network locations so communication remains reliable despite changing instances.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Service Discovery?
A runtime system for locating service instances without hardcoded addresses.
Key responsibilities
  • Store current network locations for service instances.
  • Provide health status and metadata for selection.
  • Enable clients or routers to discover healthy instances at call time.
Common misconception
Discovery is more than a directory. It must reflect liveness via health checks and may include metadata used for routing or capability checks.
Key Takeaway

Decouple logical names from IPs so services can scale and evolve independently while remaining reachable.

Runtime example
# Conceptual registration (not runnable code)
service: user-service
instance-id: user-1
address: 10.0.2.14
port: 8080
health: /health
meta: version=1.2.0

# A discovery query returns a list of healthy instances
GET /registry/user-service -> [ {instance-id:user-1, address:10.0.2.14, port:8080} ]
Analogy: think of a registry as a live phonebook with real-time status indicators rather than a printed directory that becomes stale.

screens.title: How a Service Registry Works
screens.narratorSegment: A service registry coordinates who is available and where. The typical process has three steps: registration, health checking, and discovery. First, when a service instance starts, it registers its ID, address, port, and a health-check endpoint with the registry. This can be a push registration from the instance or a pull by an agent. Second, the registry periodically invokes the health-check endpoint and updates the instance status. If health checks fail repeatedly, the registry marks the instance unhealthy so it won't be returned to callers. Third, discovery clients query the registry and receive a list of healthy instances and metadata. A concrete example is Consul: each service registers via its agent and exposes a /health path; Consul then provides APIs to list healthy nodes. A common misconception is that once registered, an instance remains valid; in reality, continuous health checks and timely deregistration are essential. Takeaway: accurate discovery depends on reliable health signaling and timely updates to the registry. How a Service Registry Works means registration + health checks + query apis keep the registry aligned with live service instances.. In practical terms, registration, health checks, and lookups that keep discovery accurate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Registry lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Registration + health checks + query APIs keep the registry aligned with live service instances.

content.html:
Process Flow
How a Service Registry Works
From registration to lookups — the lifecycle that keeps discovery current.
1
Registration
Service instances register their address, port, and health endpoint at startup, either directly or via an agent.
2
Health checks
The registry calls health endpoints periodically and updates each instance's status to prevent routing to unhealthy nodes.
3
Discovery queries
Clients or routers query the registry for healthy instances and use the returned metadata to pick a target.
Supporting details
  • Agents can manage registration on behalf of instances to avoid direct registry coupling.
  • Health checks should reflect readiness and not just liveliness to avoid routing to overloaded instances.
  • Metadata can include version, zone, or other attributes used for smarter routing.
Example: Consul
Run a Consul agent, register services via the HTTP API, and use Consul's health checks and service catalog to drive discovery.
Common mistake

Relying only on liveness checks can cause routing to instances that are alive but not ready to serve production traffic.

screens.title: Discovery Client: Roles and Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: A discovery client is the component that interacts with the registry: it registers the instance, exposes health checks, and performs lookups when the service needs to call another. In some systems the client is a library embedded in the application; in others it is an external agent that runs alongside the process. As a concrete example, a Photo Service might use a Consul client library to register itself on startup, expose a /health endpoint, and, when it needs to call the User Service, query Consul for healthy user-service instances. The client may also implement local load balancing algorithms, such as round-robin or least-connections, when multiple instances are returned. A misconception is that discovery clients only read from the registry; they are also responsible for timely deregistration and for exposing correct health semantics. The takeaway is this: a well-implemented discovery client ensures up-to-date registration and chooses healthy targets, reducing failed or misrouted calls. Question: what load-balancing strategy suits your latency profile and why? Discovery Client: Roles and Responsibilities means registers instances, performs health-aware lookups, and may apply client-side load balancing to select targets.. In practical terms, what a discovery client must do to enable reliable calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Discovery client
keyIdea.text: Registers instances, performs health-aware lookups, and may apply client-side load balancing to select targets.

content.html:
Definition
Discovery Client
Registers instances, exposes health, queries registry, and optionally balances across returned targets.
Responsibilities
  • Register and deregister instance metadata.
  • Expose readiness and liveness checks the registry can call.
  • Query registry and select a healthy instance for calls.
Agent-based clients can decouple the app from registry API changes, while embedded libraries reduce moving parts but require language support.
Concrete example
# Photo Service uses a Consul client
consul.register(service='user-service', id='user-1', address='10.0.2.14', port=8080)
# When calling User Service
instances = consul.query('user-service')
choose = round_robin(instances)
call(choose.address, choose.port, '/profile')
Pro tip

Cache discovery results briefly to reduce registry load, but honor TTLs so you don't route to dead instances.

screens.title: Client-Side Service Discovery
screens.narratorSegment: Client-side service discovery places responsibility in the calling service. The client queries a registry, receives a list of healthy instances, and applies a load-balancing strategy to select one. The advantage is fewer network hops: the client calls the target directly. A concrete example: an Order Service uses Eureka to retrieve user-service instances and uses a client-side library to do round-robin selection. This pattern also allows clients to implement sophisticated balancing strategies, like weighting by zone or version. The common misconception is that client-side is always simpler; in practice, it requires discovery logic in every client and language libraries that support the registry A P I. This can increase complexity when services are implemented in many languages. The key takeaway is that client-side discovery favors low-latency direct calls and flexible balancing, but it spreads discovery code across the system. Ask yourself: can your teams maintain discovery logic in every service and across languages? Client-Side Service Discovery means clients fetch instance lists from the registry and do their own load balancing, reducing hops but increasing client complexity.. In practical terms, clients query the registry and pick an instance directly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Clients fetch instance lists from the registry and do their own load balancing, reducing hops but increasing client complexity.

content.html:
Comparison
Client-Side Service Discovery
Client queries registry, selects an instance, then calls the service directly.
Pros
  • Fewer network hops; low call latency.
  • Clients can implement advanced load balancing.
Cons
  • Requires discovery logic in every client and language bindings.
  • More operational surface to maintain across services.
Scenario
Order Service uses Eureka + a client library. On each call it queries, filters healthy instances, and applies round-robin to select a User Service instance.
Key Takeaway

Choose client-side discovery when you need flexible client control and minimal hops, and you can manage discovery code across services.

screens.title: Server-Side Service Discovery
screens.narratorSegment: Server-side discovery removes discovery responsibility from clients. Instead, a router, reverse proxy, or load balancer queries the registry and forwards the incoming request to a healthy service instance. This pattern is common in managed environments; for example, a cloud load balancer or Kubernetes Service will handle routing and discovery for you. The client simply calls a stable router address, and the router handles instance selection. This reduces client complexity and language dependency, but it introduces an extra network hop and the potential for the router to become a bottleneck or single point of failure. A misconception is that server-side automatically means better scalability; it depends on how you architect the router: you must make it scalable and redundant. Takeaway: server-side discovery simplifies clients and supports language-agnostic services, short of exposing the system to centralized routing risks. How will you make the router highly available in your design? In practical terms, a router or load balancer queries the registry and forwards requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Comparison
Server-Side Service Discovery
Router or load balancer queries registry and forwards client requests to healthy instances.
Pros
  • Clients remain simple and language-agnostic.
  • Discovery logic centralised in the router.
Cons
  • Introduces an extra network hop and potential bottleneck.
  • Router must be highly available and monitored.
Example: Kubernetes Service
Kubernetes provides a stable virtual IP and kube-proxy routes traffic to healthy pod endpoints managed by the control plane and service registry components like etcd.
Common mistake

Treating the router as a single instance without redundancy creates a single point of failure; design for clustering or multiple router instances.

screens.title: Choosing Between Client and Server Discovery
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a discovery pattern is a design decision driven by several criteria: latency tolerance, language heterogeneity, operational burden, and the need for sophisticated client balancing. Client-side discovery reduces latency by eliminating an extra hop and enables advanced per-client strategies, but requires discovery libraries in each service and consistent implementations across languages. Server-side discovery centralizes discovery, making clients simpler and language agnostic, and can integrate with managed platforms like Kubernetes; however, it must be highly available and scalable to avoid becoming a bottleneck. A concrete decision example: if you have many polyglot teams and prefer a single routing surface, server-side simplifies operations. If you need per-client weighted routing or zone-aware balancing, client-side gives more control. A misconception is that one pattern universally beats the other; they are complementary and sometimes coexist—gateways or routers can handle public clients while internal services use client-side discovery for performance. Takeaway: choose based on operational capabilities and service topology. keyIdea.title: Selection criteria
keyIdea.text: Balance latency, operational complexity, and language support when choosing client-side or server-side discovery.

content.html:
Comparison
Choosing Between Client and Server Discovery
When to prefer client-side
  • Need for low-latency direct calls.
  • Clients can implement and maintain discovery libraries.
  • Advanced client-side balancing required.
When to prefer server-side
  • Polyglot environment where clients should remain simple.
  • You want a single routing surface for external traffic.
  • Managed platforms already provide routing/discovery primitives.
Key Takeaway

No single winner: match the pattern to your team's languages, latency needs, and operational capacity. Mixed strategies are common.

screens.title: Popular Service Registries
screens.narratorSegment: There are several widely used service registries, each with strengths that reflect different design trade-offs. ZooKeeper provides distributed coordination primitives and is often used where consistency is critical. etcd is a distributed key-value store used by Kubernetes for configuration and service metadata, favoring simplicity and strong consistency. Consul offers a service networking suite: discovery, health checks, a KV store, and DNS APIs which make it practical for many deployments. Netflix Eureka is a REST-based registry often used in JVM ecosystems with Spring Cloud. screens.title: API Gateway: Purpose and Functions
screens.narratorSegment: An A P I Gateway provides a single entry point for external clients and centralizes cross-cutting concerns. Its functions include request routing to the correct backend services, central authentication and authorization checks, rate limiting to protect backends, request and response transformation to adapt between client and service schemas, composition of multiple backend responses into one, logging and monitoring, and circuit breaking to prevent cascading failures. screens.title: API Gateway Benefits and Drawbacks
screens.narratorSegment: A P I Gateways bring important benefits but also trade-offs you must manage. Benefits include decoupling clients from many backend services so clients make a single call, centralizing authentication and authorization for consistent security, implementing rate limiting to protect back-end services, aggregating multiple responses to reduce client round trips, and centralizing logging and monitoring. An example showing benefit: a dashboard request can be a single gateway call that returns a composed response rather than several calls from the client. Drawbacks include introducing a potential single point of failure and a performance bottleneck if the gateway isn't scaled or clustered properly. Gateways also add operational complexity because they become a critical component to test, secure, and monitor. A common mistake is to push complex business logic into the gateway; this creates coupling and undermines microservice independence. Takeaway: use gateways to simplify clients and centralize cross-cutting concerns, but design them for high availability and keep business logic in the services. screens.title: Hands-on: Photo Sharing App Design
screens.narratorSegment: Let's apply these concepts in a concrete design for a photo sharing application with User, Photo, Comment, and Notification services. For service discovery we choose Consul as the registry. Each service registers on startup, exposes a /health endpoint, and Consul performs health checks so only healthy instances are returned. For client-facing traffic we deploy an A P I Gateway that handles authentication, rate limiting, and aggregation. Action one: when a mobile client requests a user's profile, it calls the gateway at GET /users/{id}. The gateway authenticates the token, finds the User Service via Consul or via its own server-side discovery integration, and returns the profile. Action two: when uploading a photo, the mobile app POSTs to /photos at the gateway; after auth and rate limiting, the gateway routes to Photo Service which may itself query Consul to call the User Service to fetch uploader metadata. Action three: Photo Service uses client-side discovery to find the User Service instance when pulling uploader details internally. A common misconception is to funnel all inter-service calls through the gateway; internal services often call each other directly for efficiency. Takeaway: combine gateway-level routing for external clients with service-level discovery for internal, latency-sensitive calls.

fullNarratorScript:
In modern microservice systems, service endpoints are fluid: instances come and go, and network addresses change continually. Service discovery is the mechanism that solves the core question: how does one service learn the current location of another? In parallel, an A P I Gateway provides a single, stable entry point for external clients, handling routing, security, aggregation, and operational controls so client code stays simple. This lesson will help you understand both concerns and why they belong in every production microservice design. We'll ground the ideas with concrete examples: how a service registers itself when it starts, how a client selects a healthy instance, and how a mobile app can ask one gateway for a dashboard composed from several services. I'll also point out common pitfalls, such as hardcoding addresses, overloading the gateway with business logic, or creating a single point of failure. By the end, you should see how service registries, discovery clients, and A P I Gateways work together to enable resilient, evolvable systems, and be ready to choose patterns that match your operational constraints.

These learning objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing distributed systems. First, you'll understand why service discovery is necessary: in dynamic microservice environments, endpoints change and hardcoding addresses creates brittle systems. Second, you'll be able to distinguish client-side and server-side discovery patterns and pick one based on language constraints, latency needs, and operational complexity. Third, you'll explain the role of a service registry and name real tools that implement this function, and you'll know how health checks keep a registry accurate. Finally on this slide, you'll start to describe the A P I Gateway's purpose: a single facade that centralizes routing, authentication, rate limiting, and aggregation. Each objective links to a competency milestone so you can verify mastery by designing a small registry and gateway configuration. Learning Objectives means master the need for discovery, the two primary patterns, the registry's responsibilities, and the gateway's role in client interactions.. In practical terms, skills you'll build in this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

On this slide we'll turn the initial objectives into applied capabilities. You'll learn to implement registration and health checks so registries reflect live instances and remove failed ones. You'll practice choosing where to place discovery logic: inside clients for flexible load balancing, or at a server router for simplicity and language agnosticism. You'll also evaluate A P I Gateway trade-offs: how centralizing authentication and aggregation improves client experience but adds operational responsibility. Finally, you'll be able to identify common mistakes, such as embedding business logic into the gateway or failing to make the gateway highly available. These applied skills prepare you to design a discovery and gateway solution for a concrete app, and to explain the trade-offs to stakeholders. Learning Objectives — Continued means implement registration and health checks, choose a discovery pattern, and plan gateway deployment to balance availability and simplicity.. In practical terms, apply discovery and gateway patterns in design choices. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Service discovery is the runtime process by which services locate each other in a distributed system. The definition is simple: instead of hardcoding IP addresses and ports, services publish where they run to a registry, and other services query that registry to learn how to reach them. This matters because microservice instances are ephemeral. They scale up and down, crash and restart, and move across hosts or containers. Without discovery, every change would require manual configuration updates, which is error-prone and slow. A concrete example is a User Service registering its address and port with a registry when it starts. An Order Service querying the registry gets a current list of healthy User Service instances and chooses one to call. A common misconception is that service discovery only stores addresses; in practice, registries also manage health checks and metadata so clients can choose healthy instances. Takeaway: discovery decouples service identity from location, enabling independent scaling and resilient connections. Consider: what operational signals will you require in health checks to avoid false positives when an instance is overloaded but not failed?

A service registry coordinates who is available and where. The typical process has three steps: registration, health checking, and discovery. First, when a service instance starts, it registers its ID, address, port, and a health-check endpoint with the registry. This can be a push registration from the instance or a pull by an agent. Second, the registry periodically invokes the health-check endpoint and updates the instance status. If health checks fail repeatedly, the registry marks the instance unhealthy so it won't be returned to callers. Third, discovery clients query the registry and receive a list of healthy instances and metadata. A concrete example is Consul: each service registers via its agent and exposes a /health path; Consul then provides APIs to list healthy nodes. A common misconception is that once registered, an instance remains valid; in reality, continuous health checks and timely deregistration are essential. Takeaway: accurate discovery depends on reliable health signaling and timely updates to the registry. How a Service Registry Works means registration + health checks + query apis keep the registry aligned with live service instances.. In practical terms, registration, health checks, and lookups that keep discovery accurate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A discovery client is the component that interacts with the registry: it registers the instance, exposes health checks, and performs lookups when the service needs to call another. In some systems the client is a library embedded in the application; in others it is an external agent that runs alongside the process. As a concrete example, a Photo Service might use a Consul client library to register itself on startup, expose a /health endpoint, and, when it needs to call the User Service, query Consul for healthy user-service instances. The client may also implement local load balancing algorithms, such as round-robin or least-connections, when multiple instances are returned. A misconception is that discovery clients only read from the registry; they are also responsible for timely deregistration and for exposing correct health semantics. The takeaway is this: a well-implemented discovery client ensures up-to-date registration and chooses healthy targets, reducing failed or misrouted calls. Client-side service discovery places responsibility in the calling service. The client queries a registry, receives a list of healthy instances, and applies a load-balancing strategy to select one. The advantage is fewer network hops: the client calls the target directly. A concrete example: an Order Service uses Eureka to retrieve user-service instances and uses a client-side library to do round-robin selection. This pattern also allows clients to implement sophisticated balancing strategies, like weighting by zone or version. Server-side discovery removes discovery responsibility from clients. Instead, a router, reverse proxy, or load balancer queries the registry and forwards the incoming request to a healthy service instance. This pattern is common in managed environments; for example, a cloud load balancer or Kubernetes Service will handle routing and discovery for you. A P I Gateways bring important benefits but also trade-offs you must manage. Benefits include decoupling clients from many backend services so clients make a single call, centralizing authentication and authorization for consistent security, implementing rate limiting to protect back-end services, aggregating multiple responses to reduce client round trips, and centralizing logging and monitoring. An example showing benefit: a dashboard request can be a single gateway call that returns a composed response rather than several calls from the client. Drawbacks include introducing a potential single point of failure and a performance bottleneck if the gateway isn't scaled or clustered properly. Gateways also add operational complexity because they become a critical component to test, secure, and monitor. A common mistake is to push complex business logic into the gateway; this creates coupling and undermines microservice independence. Takeaway: use gateways to simplify clients and centralize cross-cutting concerns, but design them for high availability and keep business logic in the services. Let's apply these concepts in a concrete design for a photo sharing application with User, Photo, Comment, and Notification services. For service discovery we choose Consul as the registry. Each service registers on startup, exposes a /health endpoint, and Consul performs health checks so only healthy instances are returned. For client-facing traffic we deploy an A P I Gateway that handles authentication, rate limiting, and aggregation. Action one: when a mobile client requests a user's profile, it calls the gateway at GET /users/{id}. The gateway authenticates the token, finds the User Service via Consul or via its own server-side discovery integration, and returns the profile. Action two: when uploading a photo, the mobile app POSTs to /photos at the gateway; after auth and rate limiting, the gateway routes to Photo Service which may itself query Consul to call the User Service to fetch uploader metadata. Action three: Photo Service uses client-side discovery to find the User Service instance when pulling uploader details internally. A common misconception is to funnel all inter-service calls through the gateway; internal services often call each other directly for efficiency. Takeaway: combine gateway-level routing for external clients with service-level discovery for internal, latency-sensitive calls.

Here are the core concepts to keep front of mind. Service discovery is the runtime process that maps logical service names to current network locations so services remain reachable as instances change. The service registry is the system that stores instance locations and health status, and popular examples include Consul, etcd, ZooKeeper, and Eureka. The discovery client registers instances, exposes health endpoints, queries the registry, and may perform local load balancing. Remember that accurate health signaling and timely deregistration are essential to prevent routing to bad instances. These three ideas are the foundation for resilient inter-service communication in microservice architectures. Finally, keep these gateway and pattern reminders in your design checklist. Client-side discovery gives clients control over instance selection and may reduce latency but requires discovery libraries in every service. Server-side discovery centralizes routing at a router or load balancer, simplifying clients but introducing an extra network hop and a component that must be made highly available. The A P I Gateway centralizes request routing, authentication and authorization, rate limiting, request/response transformation, aggregation, logging, and circuit breaking. Be careful not to overload the gateway with business logic; instead keep it focused on cross-cutting concerns and ensure you deploy it redundantly and monitor it closely. These practices reduce coupling and help your system remain resilient as it grows.
